text:
Ecology and Ecosystems
Lecture 6: Food webs, energy flow and trophic cascades

Dr Helen Marsh · School of Environmental Sciences · Michaelmas Term 2025

Learning outcomes
– Describe energy transfer between trophic levels (10% rule) and explain why food chains are short
– Distinguish top-down from bottom-up control
– Evaluate the evidence for trophic cascades: wolves in Yellowstone, sea otters and kelp forests
– Define keystone species and ecosystem engineers (beaver dams)
Reading: Begon, Townsend & Harper, chapter 17

Seminar 3 worksheet: Ecological succession

1. A glacier in Alaska has retreated over 200 years, leaving a chronosequence of sites. Describe the sequence of colonisers (lichens, mosses, Dryas, alder, spruce) and the changes in soil nitrogen along it.
2. Contrast primary and secondary succession. Which would you expect after a wildfire in a Scots pine forest?
3. Explain the facilitation, tolerance and inhibition models (Connell & Slatyer 1977).
4. Sketch how species richness changes during succession and discuss the intermediate disturbance hypothesis.

Field course report: Quadrat survey of a chalk grassland

Aim: To compare plant species diversity on a grazed and an ungrazed slope at the study site.
Methods: Fifteen 1 m x 1 m quadrats were placed along two transects using random coordinates. Percentage cover was recorded for each species using the Domin scale.
Results (draft): Simpson's diversity index was 0.82 on the grazed slope and 0.64 on the ungrazed slope. Dominant species ungrazed: upright brome (Bromopsis erecta).
To do: Add a table of species, test difference with a Mann-Whitney U test.

The Greenhouse Effect

Earth's energy balance: incoming solar 340 W/m², albedo 0.3
Greenhouse gases absorb outgoing infrared radiation: H2O, CO2, CH4, N2O
Without them the surface would average about -18 °C instead of +15 °C
Radiative forcing since 1750: CO2 +2.2 W/m²
Feedbacks: water vapour (positive), ice-albedo (positive), clouds (uncertain)
Next week: Climate models and projections (CMIP6)

Summary for Policymakers

A.1 It is unequivocal that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land. Widespread and rapid changes in the atmosphere, ocean, cryosphere and biosphere have occurred.
A.1.2 Each of the last four decades has been successively warmer than any decade that preceded it since 1850. Global surface temperature in 2011–2020 was 1.09 °C higher than in 1850–1900.
B.1 Global surface temperature will continue to increase until at least mid-century under all emissions scenarios considered.

Climate Science · Tutorial 4
Zero-dimensional energy balance model

Question 1. Using S = 1361 W/m² and albedo 0.30, derive the effective radiating temperature of the Earth.
Question 2. If doubling CO2 gives a forcing of 3.7 W/m² and the climate feedback parameter is 1.2 W/m²/K, what is the equilibrium warming?
Question 3. Explain why the ice-albedo feedback amplifies high-latitude warming.
Question 4. Discuss the difference between equilibrium climate sensitivity and transient climate response.
Hand in via the module page by Friday week 6.

Environmental Chemistry
Lecture 5: Stratospheric ozone and the Montreal Protocol

Chapman cycle: O2 + hv → 2O; O + O2 + M → O3 + M
Catalytic destruction: Cl + O3 → ClO + O2; ClO + O → Cl + O2
CFCs as source of chlorine; polar stratospheric clouds and the Antarctic ozone hole
Montreal Protocol (1987): phase-out of CFCs, HCFCs as transitional substitutes
Measure: Dobson units (1 DU = 0.01 mm of pure ozone at STP)
Prof. David Okonkwo

Problem set 2: Aquatic chemistry

1. A river water sample has pH 7.8 and total alkalinity 2.4 meq/L. Calculate the concentrations of HCO3- and CO3(2-) given pKa1 = 6.35 and pKa2 = 10.33.
2. Lake water (pH 4.5) receives acid rain. Explain why buffering capacity is lower in lakes on granite than limestone catchments.
3. Calculate the dissolved oxygen saturation at 15 °C (about 10.1 mg/L) and discuss the effect of a 5 °C temperature rise.
4. Speciation of iron: Fe(II) vs Fe(III) as a function of redox potential.

Practical 3 – Determination of lead in soil extracts by atomic absorption spectroscopy

Soil samples (1.00 g) were digested with aqua regia and diluted to 50 mL. A calibration curve was prepared with standards at 0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0 and 5.0 mg/L Pb. Absorbance was measured at 283.3 nm.
Results table: sample A 1.42 mg/L, sample B 0.38 mg/L, blank below detection limit.
Questions: calculate the Pb concentration in mg/kg soil and compare it with the UK soil guideline value of 200 mg/kg for residential land.

Hydrology and Water Resources
Lecture 4: Rainfall-runoff processes

Hydrological cycle and catchment water balance: P = Q + ET + ΔS
Infiltration: Horton overland flow vs saturation-excess flow
The storm hydrograph: rising limb, peak, recession limb; time to peak
Unit hydrograph method
Flood frequency analysis: return period T = 1/p; the 1-in-100-year flood has a 1% annual exceedance probability.
Dr Priya Raman

Workshop 2: Catchment water balance

The River Wensum catchment (area 570 km²) receives mean annual rainfall of 660 mm. Mean annual runoff measured at the gauging station is 190 mm.
a) Estimate the actual evapotranspiration, assuming no change in storage.
b) Convert the runoff to a mean discharge in m³/s.
c) Using the Penman-Monteith equation, explain which variables control potential evapotranspiration.
d) Why might actual ET be lower than potential ET in August?
Submit a one-page answer sheet at the start of next week's session.

Case study: The winter 2015–16 floods in northern England

Storm Desmond brought a record 341 mm of rain in 24 hours to Honister Pass. River levels exceeded previous maxima at Carlisle, Appleby and Kendal; more than 5,000 homes were flooded. The event raised questions about flood defences, upland land management and natural flood management (leaky dams, woodland planting).
Task: Using the hydrograph provided, estimate the return period of the peak flow and discuss the limitations of the Flood Estimation Handbook method.

Soil Science
Lecture 3: Soil texture, structure and water

Sand (2.0–0.05 mm), silt (0.05–0.002 mm), clay (< 0.002 mm); the texture triangle
Aggregates, pore space, bulk density (typical 1.3 g/cm³)
Field capacity and permanent wilting point; available water capacity
Cation exchange capacity of clay minerals and organic matter
Soil horizons O, A, E, B, C
Dr Tom Ashworth

Soil Science Practical 2: pH and organic matter by loss on ignition

Weigh 10 g of air-dried soil (< 2 mm) into a beaker and add 25 mL deionised water. Stir, leave for 30 minutes and measure pH with a calibrated electrode. For organic matter, heat 5 g of oven-dried soil in a crucible at 450 °C for four hours in the muffle furnace.
Calculation: % LOI = (mass lost / initial dry mass) × 100.
Compare topsoil from woodland, arable and grassland sites. Why does pH differ?

Soil erosion by water and wind

Globally, an estimated 24 billion tonnes of fertile soil are lost every year. The Universal Soil Loss Equation (USLE) predicts annual loss as A = R · K · LS · C · P, where R is rainfall erosivity, K soil erodibility, LS slope length and steepness, C cover management and P conservation practice. Conservation measures include contour ploughing, cover crops, no-till farming and hedgerows. Discuss which factor is easiest for a farmer to modify.

Environmental Policy and Law
Lecture 7: From Kyoto to Paris

1992 UNFCCC: common but differentiated responsibilities
1997 Kyoto Protocol: binding targets for Annex I countries
2015 Paris Agreement: nationally determined contributions (NDCs), 1.5 °C aspiration, five-year stocktake
Policy instruments: carbon tax vs emissions trading scheme (EU ETS, UK ETS)
Polluter pays principle; precautionary principle
Dr Olivia Grant

Coursework 2 essay plan: "Critically evaluate the UK's net zero target for 2050"

Introduction: Climate Change Act 2008 (amended 2019), carbon budgets set by the Climate Change Committee.
Section 1: Progress so far (power sector decarbonisation, coal phase-out).
Section 2: Hard-to-abate sectors: aviation, agriculture, heating.
Section 3: Policy tools and gaps: contracts for difference, heat pump grants, planning.
Section 4: Equity and public acceptance.
Word count: 2,500. Deadline: 12 January 2026.

Governance and the environment: key concepts

Command-and-control regulation sets legally enforceable standards, e.g. emission limits. Market-based instruments use prices to change behaviour. Voluntary agreements rely on industry self-regulation. Environmental justice asks who bears the costs of pollution and who benefits from environmental goods. The Aarhus Convention gives the public rights of access to information, participation in decision-making and access to justice in environmental matters.
Seminar question: Why is enforcement often weaker than the law on paper?

Environmental Statistics · Practical 4
Linear regression in R

The file lakes.csv holds total phosphorus (µg/L) and chlorophyll-a (µg/L) for 48 lakes.
1. Plot chlorophyll-a against phosphorus; log10-transform both variables if needed.
2. Fit a model with lm(log_chl ~ log_tp, data = lakes). Interpret the slope and R².
3. Check residuals (plot(model)): normality, constant variance, outliers.
4. Predict chlorophyll-a at 30 µg/L phosphorus with a 95% prediction interval.
Submit your R script and a one-page write-up.

Lecture 8: Analysis of variance

One-way ANOVA tests whether three or more group means differ. Total variation is partitioned into between-group and within-group sums of squares: F = MS_between / MS_within.
Assumptions: independence, normally distributed residuals, homogeneity of variance (Levene's test).
Post-hoc comparisons: Tukey HSD.
Non-parametric alternative: Kruskal–Wallis.
Example: Invertebrate abundance in streams above, at and below a sewage outfall.

Revision notes: sampling design

Simple random, systematic and stratified sampling; when to use each. Pseudoreplication: treating subsamples as independent replicates (Hurlbert 1984). Sample size and power: smaller effects require larger n. Type I and Type II errors. p-values are not the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
Past paper question: A researcher takes 10 water samples from a single pond and 10 from another and concludes ponds differ. What is the problem?

GIS and Remote Sensing · Practical 5
Vector analysis in QGIS

Load the shapefiles rivers.shp, sssi.shp (Sites of Special Scientific Interest) and landuse.shp. Reproject all layers to British National Grid (EPSG:27700).
1. Create a 100 m buffer around rivers.
2. Intersect the buffer with the landuse layer to find arable fields within 100 m of a watercourse.
3. Calculate the total area in hectares (field calculator: $area / 10000).
4. Produce a map layout with scale bar, north arrow and legend.

Remote sensing: vegetation indices and land cover classification

NDVI = (NIR − Red) / (NIR + Red); healthy vegetation 0.6–0.9
Sentinel-2 bands: red (665 nm), NIR (842 nm), 10 m resolution
Supervised classification: training areas, maximum likelihood, random forest
Accuracy assessment: confusion matrix, overall accuracy, kappa coefficient
Case study: monitoring deforestation in the Amazon with Landsat time series

Lab sheet: Georeferencing and coordinate systems

Aim: to georeference a scanned 1:10,000 Ordnance Survey map and to understand the difference between geographic and projected coordinate systems.
Step 1 Add the raster in the Georeferencer. Step 2 Choose at least six ground control points (road junctions, church towers). Step 3 Transformation type: polynomial 1. Step 4 Check the RMSE (aim for less than one pixel).
Question: Why does a degree of longitude cover a smaller distance at 55°N than at the equator?

Energy and Sustainability
Lecture 5: Renewable electricity

Wind: P = ½ ρ A v³ cp, Betz limit cp ≤ 0.593
Offshore wind in the North Sea: capacity factors above 45%
Solar PV: efficiency of silicon cells ~20%, UK capacity factor ~11%
Intermittency, grid balancing, storage options (pumped hydro, batteries, hydrogen)
Levelised cost of electricity (LCOE) comparison
Prof. Alan Whitcombe

Tutorial 3: Carbon footprint calculation

Calculate the annual carbon footprint of a household using these data:
- Electricity: 2,900 kWh (grid intensity 0.21 kg CO2e/kWh)
- Natural gas: 12,000 kWh (0.18 kg CO2e/kWh)
- Car: 8,000 miles at 0.27 kg CO2e/mile
- Return flight London–New York: 1.9 t CO2e
Compare your result with the UK average of 5.5 t per person per year and suggest three options to reduce emissions, with estimated savings.

Life cycle assessment of reusable versus single-use coffee cups

Goal and scope: Functional unit is the serving of 1,000 hot drinks. System boundary covers raw material extraction, manufacturing, transport, use (including washing) and end of life.
Inventory: Single-use cup 11 g paper + 1.5 g polyethylene lining; reusable ceramic cup 330 g, used 500 times.
Impact categories: global warming potential (kg CO2e), water use, waste.
Interpretation (to complete): break-even number of uses.

Conservation Biology
Lecture 4: Assessing extinction risk

IUCN Red List categories: LC, NT, VU, EN, CR, EW, EX
Criteria A–E: population decline, geographic range, small population size, quantitative analysis
Drivers: habitat loss, overexploitation, invasive species, pollution, climate change
Population viability analysis; minimum viable population
The extinction vortex: inbreeding depression, demographic stochasticity
Dr Ellie Watkins

Case study: reintroducing beavers to Britain

Eurasian beavers (Castor fiber) were hunted to extinction in Britain by the 16th century. A trial reintroduction began on the River Otter in Devon in 2015 and found benefits for flood attenuation, water quality and amphibians. Landowners raised concerns over damage to trees and crops. In 2022 the government licensed wild releases in England.
Questions: Who are the stakeholders? What monitoring would you propose? Consider genetic diversity of the founder population.

MacArthur and Wilson's equilibrium theory of island biogeography predicts that species richness on an island results from a balance between immigration and extinction rates. Large islands near the mainland support more species than small, remote ones. The species–area relationship S = cA^z with z typically 0.2–0.35 underlies estimates that habitat loss will drive many extinctions. SLOSS debate: is a single large reserve better than several small ones?

Environmental Impact Assessment
Lecture 3: Screening and scoping

Stages of EIA: screening → scoping → baseline studies → impact prediction → mitigation → Environmental Statement → decision → monitoring
Screening: Schedule 1 projects always need EIA; Schedule 2 depends on thresholds and sensitive locations
Scoping: identify significant effects, consult statutory bodies (Natural England, Environment Agency)
Mitigation hierarchy: avoid, reduce, compensate
Dr Rachel Penrose

Group project brief: EIA for a proposed 12-turbine onshore wind farm

Your team acts as environmental consultants. The site is an upland moor with blanket bog, a nearby SPA for hen harrier, and a village 1.2 km away.
Deliverables: (1) scoping report, (2) baseline survey plan covering ecology, noise, landscape and visual impact, hydrology, (3) summary of predicted impacts using a significance matrix, (4) mitigation and monitoring plan. 20-minute presentation in week 11. Weighting 40% of module mark.

Coursework: critique of an Environmental Statement

Select a published Environmental Statement for a development of your choice and evaluate it against the criteria of the Lee and Colley review package: description of the development, baseline, scoping, impact prediction, mitigation, non-technical summary. Identify where uncertainty has been acknowledged. Word limit 2,000. Submit through the module page by 4 pm on Friday.

Pollution and Waste Management
Lecture 6: The waste hierarchy and landfill

Waste hierarchy: prevention, preparing for re-use, recycling, other recovery (energy), disposal
UK municipal recycling rate ~44% (2022); landfill tax £103.70 per tonne
Landfill: liners, leachate collection, landfill gas (≈50% CH4), capping
Anaerobic digestion and composting of biowaste
Energy from waste: incineration with heat recovery
Dr Mark Fenwick

Practical 4: urban air quality

You are given hourly NO2 and PM2.5 data for a roadside monitoring station in Manchester for 2024.
1. Calculate annual means and compare with the WHO guideline (10 µg/m³ NO2, 5 µg/m³ PM2.5) and the UK limit value (40 µg/m³ NO2).
2. Identify the number of hours exceeding 200 µg/m³ NO2 (limit: 18 allowed per year).
3. Plot diurnal and weekly profiles and relate them to traffic.
4. Discuss the benefits of a Clean Air Zone.

Remediation of contaminated land

Techniques are grouped into excavation and disposal, in situ treatment and containment. Bioremediation uses microorganisms to degrade hydrocarbons, while phytoremediation uses plants such as willow or sunflower to extract heavy metals. Pump-and-treat systems remove contaminated groundwater but may take decades. Risk-based land management follows the source–pathway–receptor model: remediation is only needed where all three are present.
